title: Abuse beyond the bruise
subtitle: The statutory definition of abuse and civil protection under the Family Law Act 1996
objectives: State the statutory definition of abusive behaviour under s 1 Domestic Abuse Act 2021, including economic abuse and controlling or coercive behaviour
Distinguish a non-molestation order from an occupation order and identify who may apply for each under Part IV Family Law Act 1996
Explain how civil protection proceedings and a parallel criminal prosecution for the same conduct can run alongside one another

leadingAuthorities.role: The first statutory definition of domestic abuse in England and Wales, extending expressly to economic and controlling or coercive behaviour
The civil protection framework: non-molestation orders (s 42) and occupation orders (ss 33, 35–38)

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students can define 'abuse' as violence and stop there. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You know the headline definition — this lesson checks whether you can spot abuse in a fact pattern that never mentions a single act of violence.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans on scenario questions involving economic control and coercive behaviour, not textbook definitions — expect facts that don't announce themselves as 'abuse'.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and learn the five categories in s 1 DAA 2021 precisely — later parts assume you can name them without prompting, especially the distinction between economic abuse and controlling or coercive behaviour.

overview.hook: No one hits her. He controls every pound she spends, checks her phone, decides which friends she's allowed to see, and tells her often enough that she starts to believe it herself. For most of English legal history, the law had almost nothing to say about this. Since 2021 it has a name, a statutory definition, and a route into court that doesn't require a single visible injury. This lesson is about what the law now recognises as abuse, and the two civil orders that exist to protect someone from it — quite apart from whatever the criminal law is doing about the same conduct.

parts.heading: Defining abuse: five categories, not one
parts.voice: structural — sets out the statutory framework students will return to
body: Before the Domestic Abuse Act 2021, English law had no single statutory definition of domestic abuse at all — the concept was built up piecemeal, largely around physical violence, across criminal offences, housing law and the family courts' own practice guidance. Section 1 of the 2021 Act changes that: it supplies a single, cross-cutting statutory definition that now anchors civil protection, housing priority, and a range of other statutory contexts.

The definition has two building blocks. First, the parties must be "personally connected" — broadly, intimate partners or ex-partners, family members, or people who share parental responsibility for a child, as defined in s 2. Second, the behaviour itself must fall within one of five categories the Act lists: physical or sexual abuse; violent or threatening behaviour; controlling or coercive behaviour; economic abuse; and psychological, emotional or other abuse. Crucially, s 1 makes clear it does not matter whether the behaviour is a single incident or a course of conduct — a single act can be abuse, though a course of conduct is often what proves controlling or coercive behaviour in practice.

The two categories students most often underweight are economic abuse and controlling or coercive behaviour, because neither requires anything that looks, on its face, like violence. This lesson spends real time on both, because exam fact patterns are increasingly built around them precisely to test whether a student's mental model of 'abuse' has moved past physical harm.

components.definition: Under s 1(4) Domestic Abuse Act 2021, any behaviour that has a substantial adverse effect on a person's ability to acquire, use or maintain money or other property, or to obtain goods or services — for example, controlling household income, running up debt in a partner's name, or sabotaging their ability to work.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that the statutory definition of abuse under s 1 Domestic Abuse Act 2021 requires an element of physical violence?
sliderLabels: Definitely does not require physical violence
interaction.explanation: It does not. Section 1 lists five categories of abusive behaviour, and physical or sexual abuse is only one of them — economic abuse and controlling or coercive behaviour are equally within the statutory definition, with no requirement that any physical act ever occurs.

parts.heading: Reading s 1 closely: what the Act actually says
parts.voice: statute-first — works from the text outward
body: It's worth reading s 1 in something close to its own words, because exam questions often ask you to classify a scenario against the exact statutory categories rather than a paraphrase of them.

Section 1(3) lists the categories of abusive behaviour. Section 1(4) then defines economic abuse specifically, because Parliament recognised it as a distinct and under-recognised form of control — one that can trap a person in a relationship long after any other form of abuse would have prompted them to leave, by leaving them with no money, no credit history of their own, or no means of independent housing.

Controlling or coercive behaviour sits alongside economic abuse as its own category, and the two often overlap in practice: controlling access to money is frequently one tactic within a wider pattern of controlling or coercive behaviour, which can also include isolating someone from friends and family, monitoring their movements or communications, or instilling fear through repeated degradation — none of which needs to involve a threat of physical harm to count.

components.text: Behaviour is 'abusive' if it consists of any of the following — (a) physical or sexual abuse; (b) violent or threatening behaviour; (c) controlling or coercive behaviour; (d) economic abuse; (e) psychological, emotional or other abuse; and it does not matter whether the behaviour consists of a single incident or a course of conduct. Economic abuse means any behaviour that has a substantial adverse effect on B's ability to — (a) acquire, use or maintain money or other property, or (b) obtain goods or services.
elements: Economic abuse — substantial adverse effect on acquiring, using or maintaining money, property, goods or services
Applies to a single incident or a course of conduct

interaction.prompt: Under s 1 Domestic Abuse Act 2021, is a single incident capable of amounting to abuse, or must there always be a course of conduct?
options: A single incident can amount to abuse — the Act expressly says it does not matter whether behaviour is a single incident or a course of conduct
There must always be a course of conduct; one incident is never enough
Only economic abuse can consist of a single incident
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Section 1(3) is explicit that a single incident is capable of being abusive — though in practice, controlling or coercive behaviour is usually evidenced by a pattern, since control by its nature tends to be exercised repeatedly.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at the closing words of s 1(3) — the Act says directly that it does not matter whether the behaviour is a single incident or a course of conduct. Course-of-conduct evidence is common in practice, especially for controlling or coercive behaviour, but it isn't a legal requirement.

parts.heading: Occupation orders: who stays, who leaves
parts.voice: structural — reference-style, building the framework the rest of the lesson assumes
body: An occupation order regulates who lives in the family home, and it can go as far as excluding a respondent from the home — and sometimes a defined area around it — even where the respondent owns or has a legal right to occupy the property. This is a significant intrusion on ordinary property rights, and the Act structures the court's power carefully around the applicant's entitlement.

Section 33 is the core provision for an applicant who is themselves "entitled" to occupy the home — typically because they own it, rent it, or have a beneficial interest, or have matrimonial/civil partnership home rights. The court can declare, enforce, restrict or regulate the applicant's occupation rights, and can go further and require the respondent to leave the home, or part of it, or stay out of a defined surrounding area.

Whether to make an order, and on what terms, often turns on the "balance of harm" test: the court considers the likely effect of making (or not making) the order on the health, safety and wellbeing of the applicant and any relevant child, weighed against the effect on the respondent. Where making no order would cause the applicant or a child significant harm attributable to the respondent's conduct, and that harm is as great as or greater than any harm to the respondent from making the order, the court must make it — this can tip a case that might otherwise be finely balanced towards an order plainly weighted to protect the applicant.

components.label: Occupation orders under s 33 FLA 1996 — the shape of the test
points: Available to an applicant "entitled" to occupy the home (owner, tenant, or beneficial/home-rights interest)
The court can regulate occupation, or go further and exclude the respondent from the home and a defined surrounding area
The balance of harm test weighs the effect on the applicant/child of refusing an order against the effect on the respondent of making one
Where significant harm to the applicant or child, attributable to the respondent's conduct, outweighs harm to the respondent, the court must make an order

interaction.prompt: Put these steps in the order a court works through on a s 33 occupation order application.
items: Confirm the applicant is entitled to occupy the home
Identify the range of orders available, from regulating occupation up to excluding the respondent
Assess the likely harm to the applicant and any child if no order is made
Weigh that harm against the likely harm to the respondent if an order is made, applying the balance of harm test
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the structure: entitlement first, then the available range of orders, then the balance of harm test that decides whether — and how far — the court should go.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — entitlement is the threshold gateway question, the available orders come next, and the balance of harm assessment is the substantive test that decides the outcome, not the starting point.

parts.heading: Non-molestation orders: a wider net, a lower bar to apply
parts.voice: case-narrative — grounds the doctrine in how it plays out
body: A non-molestation order under s 42 is narrower in its effect than an occupation order — it doesn't touch who lives where — but wider in what it can prohibit and easier to obtain, because it doesn't depend on any property entitlement at all. "Molestation" is not exhaustively defined in the Act, and the courts have deliberately kept it broad: it covers not only violence but harassment, pestering, and any conduct calculated to cause distress, including a persistent pattern of unwanted contact, threats, or intimidation that falls short of assault.

Consider a scenario built from this pattern: a woman ends a relationship, and her former partner, who has never struck her, begins turning up uninvited at her workplace, sending dozens of messages a day, and telling mutual friends she is mentally unstable in an apparent effort to isolate her. None of this needs to be physical to justify an order — s 42's language is drafted precisely to capture a course of conduct like this, and it sits comfortably within the DAA 2021 s 1 categories of controlling or coercive behaviour and psychological abuse covered in Part 2.

Anyone "associated" with the respondent may apply — a wider category than "entitled" under s 33, covering (among others) spouses, civil partners, cohabitants and former cohabitants, people who have had an intimate relationship of significant duration, and relatives. The court considers all the circumstances, including the need to secure the health, safety and wellbeing of the applicant and any relevant child, and can make the order on the balance of the evidence presented — including, in urgent cases, without notice to the respondent, with a return hearing to follow.

components.definition: The wider category of applicant eligible for a non-molestation order under Part IV FLA 1996, including spouses, civil partners, cohabitants and former cohabitants, people who have had an intimate personal relationship of significant duration, and relatives — deliberately broader than the property-based 'entitled' category used for occupation orders.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that most clearly supports an application for a non-molestation order.
interaction.scenarioText: Maya ended a six-month relationship with Daniel two weeks ago. Daniel has never been physically violent towards her. Since the breakup he has sent her over thirty messages a day, waited outside her flat on three occasions, and told several of her friends that she is 'losing her mind' in an apparent attempt to turn them against her.
tappableSpans: sent her over thirty messages a day, waited outside her flat
told several of her friends that she is 'losing her mind'
interaction.correctSpan: sent her over thirty messages a day, waited outside her flat
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the harassing course of conduct s 42 is built to capture — persistent unwanted contact and monitoring, calculated to cause distress, regardless of the absence of any physical violence.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the sustained pattern of unwanted contact and pursuit, rather than the relationship's length or the absence of violence. 'Molestation' under s 42 is read broadly and doesn't require any physical act at all.

parts.heading: Two tracks at once: civil protection and criminal proceedings
parts.voice: reflective — closes the lesson by locating it within the wider system
body: The same conduct that grounds a non-molestation or occupation order can also be a criminal offence — controlling or coercive behaviour has been a standalone offence since the Serious Crime Act 2015, and physical violence or threats will often amount to assault or a harassment offence in their own right. Students sometimes assume these two routes are alternatives, and that a victim (or the state) must pick one. They aren't, and they don't.

Civil protection and criminal proceedings serve different purposes and run on different tracks, often simultaneously. A non-molestation order is a civil injunction, obtained on the civil standard of proof (the balance of probabilities), aimed at preventing future harm through a court order with its own enforcement mechanism — breach of a non-molestation order is itself a criminal offence, giving the civil order real teeth. A criminal prosecution, by contrast, is brought by the state, proved to the criminal standard (beyond reasonable doubt), and aimed at punishing past conduct, not primarily at preventing future contact — though a criminal court can also impose its own protective measures, such as a restraining order, on conviction or even on acquittal in some circumstances.

In practice, this means a family court and a criminal court can be dealing with the same underlying facts at the same time, applying different standards of proof to different questions, without either proceeding depending on the outcome of the other. A family court is not required to wait for a criminal trial to conclude before deciding whether protection is needed now — and given the lower civil standard, an order can be made even where a criminal case has not been brought, has stalled, or has resulted in acquittal.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often assume a family court must wait for a criminal prosecution over the same conduct to conclude before it can make a non-molestation or occupation order, or that an acquittal means a civil order cannot be made.
components.whyItsWrong: The two proceedings serve different purposes, use different standards of proof, and are not sequentially dependent. A family court can and often does act immediately on the civil standard of probability to protect someone from future harm, regardless of the pace, progress, or outcome of any parallel criminal case.

interaction.prompt: Which scenario shows the civil and criminal tracks operating correctly, in parallel, rather than one improperly blocking the other?
interaction.scenarioA: A family court refuses to consider a non-molestation order application because a police investigation into the same conduct is ongoing and has not yet concluded.
interaction.scenarioB: A family court grants a non-molestation order based on the applicant's evidence on the balance of probabilities, while a separate criminal investigation into the same conduct continues independently.
interaction.explanation: B is correct: civil protection is decided on the civil standard, independently of the pace or outcome of any criminal process. A describes an error — there is no rule requiring a family court to pause pending a criminal investigation or prosecution over the same facts.

testPool.prompt: Name the five categories of abusive behaviour listed in s 1(3) Domestic Abuse Act 2021.
acceptableAnswers: physical or sexual abuse, violent or threatening behaviour, controlling or coercive behaviour, economic abuse, psychological/emotional or other abuse
testPool.modelAnswer: Physical or sexual abuse; violent or threatening behaviour; controlling or coercive behaviour; economic abuse; and psychological, emotional or other abuse.

testPool.prompt: Name the two civil orders available under Part IV Family Law Act 1996.
testPool.modelAnswer: A non-molestation order (s 42) and an occupation order (s 33 and related sections).

testPool.prompt: Under s 1(4) DAA 2021, is economic abuse limited to behaviour affecting a person's access to money, or does it extend further?
options: It extends further — it also covers a substantial adverse effect on obtaining goods or services, and acquiring or maintaining property
It is limited strictly to control over cash and bank accounts

testPool.prompt: Must an applicant own or rent the home to apply for a non-molestation order under s 42?
options: No — eligibility turns on being an 'associated person', not on any property entitlement
Yes — the same entitlement test used for occupation orders applies

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT, on its own, sufficient for a court to refuse to consider a non-molestation order application?
options: The respondent has never used physical violence against the applicant
A parallel police investigation into the same conduct is ongoing
Both of the above are, correctly, not sufficient grounds for refusal
testPool.trapExplanation: Neither the absence of physical violence nor an ongoing parallel criminal investigation is a bar to a non-molestation order. 'Molestation' extends well beyond violence, and civil and criminal proceedings run independently — so both listed reasons are, correctly, insufficient to refuse the application.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best describes the relationship between a non-molestation order and a criminal prosecution for the same conduct?
options: The civil order is decided on the balance of probabilities and aims to prevent future harm; the criminal case is decided beyond reasonable doubt and aims to punish past conduct — the two can run in parallel
A criminal conviction must be obtained first before a non-molestation order can be made
A non-molestation order automatically triggers a criminal prosecution for the same conduct
testPool.trapExplanation: The tempting wrong answers imagine a sequential or automatic relationship between the two tracks. In fact they are structurally independent — different standards of proof, different purposes, and no requirement that one precede or trigger the other.

testPool.prompt: In the extract from s 1(3) Domestic Abuse Act 2021 below, highlight the clause that confirms a single incident can amount to abuse.
testPool.passage: Behaviour is 'abusive' if it consists of any of the following — (a) physical or sexual abuse; (b) violent or threatening behaviour; (c) controlling or coercive behaviour; (d) economic abuse; (e) psychological, emotional or other abuse; and it does not matter whether the behaviour consists of a single incident or a course of conduct.
testPool.ratioSentence: it does not matter whether the behaviour consists of a single incident or a course of conduct

testPool.prompt: In the extract from s 1(4) below, highlight the phrase that sets the threshold for conduct to count as economic abuse.
testPool.passage: Economic abuse means any behaviour that has a substantial adverse effect on B's ability to acquire, use or maintain money or other property, or obtain goods or services.
testPool.ratioSentence: a substantial adverse effect on B's ability to acquire, use or maintain money or other property, or obtain goods or services

testPool.prompt: A partner opens credit cards in his girlfriend's name without her knowledge, runs up significant debt on them, and refuses to let her see the household bank statements. How confident are you that this falls within the statutory definition of economic abuse?
testPool.explanation: This is a textbook example: running up debt in her name and denying her access to financial information both have a substantial adverse effect on her ability to acquire, use or maintain money — precisely what s 1(4) is designed to capture.

testPool.prompt: Under the s 33 balance of harm test, what must the court do once it finds that refusing an order would cause the applicant or a relevant child significant harm attributable to the respondent's conduct, at least as great as any harm to the respondent from making the order?
options: It must make the occupation order
It has an unfettered discretion whether to make the order
It must refer the matter to the criminal court first

testPool.prompt: Priya jointly owns her home with her husband. He has never been physically violent, but he controls all her money, monitors her phone constantly, and forbids her from seeing her sister. She wants him to leave the home and wants an order preventing this behaviour. Which order(s) should her application target?
options: Both an occupation order (s 33, since she is entitled as joint owner) and a non-molestation order (s 42, to prohibit the controlling behaviour)
Only a non-molestation order, since occupation orders require physical violence
Only an occupation order, since non-molestation orders cannot address controlling behaviour
testPool.explanation: As a joint owner she is entitled to apply for an occupation order to address who lives in the home, and separately a non-molestation order can prohibit the controlling and coercive behaviour directly — the two orders address different problems and are not mutually exclusive.

testPool.prompt: A woman rents a flat solely in her own name. Her adult brother, who does not live there but visits regularly, has begun repeatedly threatening her when he visits and demanding money. Can she apply for civil protection under Part IV FLA 1996?
options: Yes — as a relative, she is an 'associated person' eligible to apply for a non-molestation order, regardless of who holds the tenancy
No — Part IV only protects intimate partners, not other family members
No — since he does not live there, an occupation order is her only option and it would fail
testPool.explanation: Relatives fall within the 'associated persons' category for a non-molestation order under s 42, and cohabitation is not required for that order — an occupation order would be a different question given entitlement, but it isn't the only route available here.

testPool.prompt: Tom and his wife jointly own their home. Tom has never struck her, but he decides how much money she may spend each week, checks her phone daily, and has told her repeatedly that no one would believe her if she complained. She applies for an occupation order and a non-molestation order. Analyse whether the statutory definition of abuse is met and whether she has standing for each order.
factsToOrder: Tom controls his wife's weekly spending
Tom repeatedly tells her she would not be believed
She is a joint owner of the home

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student applies it to the facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Tom's conduct meets the s 1 DAA 2021 definition of abuse, and whether his wife has standing for an occupation order and a non-molestation order.
modelAnswer.rule: Section 1(3) DAA 2021 defines abuse to include economic abuse and controlling or coercive behaviour, without requiring violence. An occupation order under s 33 requires the applicant to be entitled to occupy the home; a non-molestation order under s 42 requires only that the parties are associated persons.
modelAnswer.application: Controlling weekly spending is economic abuse under s 1(4); monitoring her phone and undermining her credibility are controlling or coercive and psychological abuse under s 1(3)(c) and (e). As a joint owner, she is entitled to apply for an occupation order regarding who occupies the home; as a spouse, she is plainly an associated person and eligible for a non-molestation order regardless of her property interest.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Tom's conduct meets the statutory definition of abuse despite the absence of any violence, and she has standing to apply for both orders — the occupation order to address the home, and the non-molestation order to prohibit the ongoing controlling behaviour.

testPool.prompt: Order these correctly, from the least property-dependent route to the most property-dependent route into civil protection under Part IV FLA 1996.
items: Non-molestation order — available to any 'associated person', regardless of any property interest
Occupation order for an 'entitled' applicant — requires ownership, tenancy, or a beneficial/home-rights interest
Exclusion from the home and a defined surrounding area under an occupation order — the most intrusive order available, still requiring entitlement

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating 'abuse' as synonymous with physical violence, and assuming civil protection proceedings must wait on a parallel criminal case. Both errors collapse under a close reading of s 1 DAA 2021 and the independence of the two tracks.
